clinical_knowledge.topic: Severe Mitral Regurgitation with Congestive Heart Failure evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Severe Mitral Regurgitation with Congestive Heart Failure is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Chronic severe MR causes progressive left atrial and ventricular volume overload; new or worsening heart failure symptoms in a known MR patient signal decompensation and the need for urgent evaluation for valve repair or replacement.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Severe Mitral Regurgitation with Congestive Heart Failure.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Aortic stenosis with secondary heart failure without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Coughing up pink frothy sputum — suggests acute pulmonary edema needing urgent management.
management_principles: Assess severity clinically and confirm the valve lesion with imaging before deciding on definitive therapy
Treat suspected acute pulmonary edema urgently with oxygen if hypoxemic, ventilatory support as needed, and IV loop diuresis; determine the valve lesion and longer-term therapy after stabilization
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Severe Mitral Regurgitation with congestive heart failure. progressive shortness of breath when lying flat, coughing up pink spit, and heart murmur. 58M reports progressive shortness of breath over 2 months, worsening significantly when lying flat in bed (orthopnea requiring 3 pillows). Also complains of fatigue and coughing up frothy, pink-tinged sputum.
reference_soap.objective: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Severe Mitral Regurgitation with congestive heart failure.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute decompensated heart failure with possible pulmonary edema; transthoracic echocardiography is needed to determine whether severe mitral regurgitation is present and its mechanism.
reference_soap.plan: Urgently assess and stabilize suspected acute pulmonary edema. Give oxygen if hypoxemic, use ventilatory support as needed, and administer IV loop diuresis while monitoring haemodynamics. Order transthoracic echocardiogram. If severe mitral regurgitation is confirmed, refer to a valve team for repair-versus-replacement assessment after stabilization. Refer to specialty team and provide comprehensive patient counseling.

Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for cardiothoracic surgery
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies for Severe Mitral Regurgitation with congestive heart failure.

teaching.diagnosis: Severe Mitral Regurgitation with Congestive Heart Failure
teaching.one_liner: Chronic backward leakage through a damaged mitral valve overloads the left atrium and lungs, causing progressive orthopnea, fatigue, and pink frothy sputum — needs echocardiographic evaluation for valve repair or replacement.
differentials: Aortic stenosis with secondary heart failure
red_flags: Coughing up pink frothy sputum — suggests acute pulmonary edema needing urgent management

history.answer: I have been having terrible shortness of breath, especially when I lie flat, and I recently started coughing up pink frothy spit.
It started gradually about two months ago, but it has gotten noticeably worse over the past week.
At first I only felt winded climbing stairs, but now I get breathless just walking across a room or even sitting still.
The shortness of breath is continuous throughout the day, and I have never experienced anything this severe before.
I cannot sleep flat at all and have to prop myself up with three pillows, and I often wake up in the middle of the night gasping for air.
Walking around and lying flat make it much worse, while sitting straight up in a chair gives me a little relief.
I sometimes hear a slight rattling or wheezing sound in my chest when I breathe hard, but it mostly feels like drowning.
I have had a worsening wet cough for the last few days, but I have had no fever or chills at all.
No, I have not had any pressure, tightness, or sharp stabbing pains in my chest.
My heart feels like it races when I struggle for air, but I have not had lightheadedness or blackouts.
The spit is bubbly, thin, and pinkish in color, not thick yellow phlegm or solid blood clots.
My shoes feel slightly tight around my ankles by the evening, and my weight has gone up by about four pounds.
Neither leg is swollen or painful on its own, and I have not had any long flights, cast immobilizations, or recent operations.

history.answer: I feel completely exhausted and drained of energy, but I have not had pale skin, black stools, or unusual bleeding.
I do feel anxious because it is so hard to breathe, but my hands, feet, and mouth are not tingling or numb.
A doctor told me ten years ago that I had mitral valve prolapse, but I have never had asthma, COPD, or a heart attack.
No, I have never been prescribed an inhaler and have never used one.
No, I do not take blood pressure pills, pain medicines, beta-blockers, or any other regular medications.
No, I work in a regular office and have not been exposed to dust, asbestos, birds, or mold.
I was wondering if I developed sudden asthma or if my heart might be failing.
I am really frightened that my heart valve has torn or suffered serious damage.
I want you to check my heart valve right away and give me treatment so I can breathe again.
Other than the mitral valve prolapse diagnosed a decade ago, I have had no high blood pressure, diabetes, or other chronic illnesses.
I had my appendix removed when I was sixteen, but I have had no other surgeries or hospitalizations.
I am not taking any prescription drugs, over-the-counter medications, or herbal supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products in my life.
I only have an occasional glass of beer or wine once or twice a year at celebrations.
I work as an office clerk sitting at a desk, and I live at home with my wife.
My father had high blood pressure in his old age, but no one in my family had heart valve disorders or died suddenly.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 135/85 mmHg, heart rate is 98 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation is 92% on ambient air, and body temperature is 36.7 degrees Celsius.
The patient is tachypneic and visibly distressed when recumbent, with intercostal retractions and without cyanosis or digital clubbing.
Jugular venous pulse is elevated to 4 cm above the sternal angle at 45 degrees.
Hyperdynamic apical impulse displaced laterally to the sixth intercostal space at the anterior axillary line, accompanied by an apical systolic thrill.
Percussion note is dull at both lung bases and resonant across the upper and middle lung fields.
Prominent bilateral inspiratory crackles extending across the lower halves of both lung fields, without wheezing.
Regular rhythm with a soft first heart sound, an audible third heart sound, and a grade 4/6 holosystolic murmur heard best at the apex and radiating to the left axilla.
Abdomen is soft and non-tender, with mild hepatomegaly palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin and no ascites.
Mild 1+ bilateral pitting edema noted over both lower ankles and pretibial areas.
Both calves are symmetric without calf tenderness, erythema, warmth, or palpable venous cord.
